line: Could you even tell if a song was AI?
frame0: BLIND TEST: 97% COULDN'T TELL. COULD YOU?
emotion: Pride, poked. Almost everyone is sure they would hear it. So a true stat, that 97% of 9,000 people failed a blind test, makes you doubt your own ears for a second and want to test yourself or argue in the comments. It is the question everyone is already asking, put to you.
backing: FL 5.1 (VERIFIED: 9,000 adults in 8 countries, 3 tracks, 97% failed; safe: 'In a blind test, 97% of 9,000 people couldn't tell which songs were AI'); FL 8.7 (keep 'blind test' on screen, never a universal claim). The turn to money rests on FL 3.1-3.3, 3.11, 2.4, 4.1-4.2, 4.10, 8.2 and 8.5.
fixes: Keep; credit 'Deezer/Ipsos, 2025' small on frame 0 and turn to fake plays by line 2.
notes: The best ride on the fuss and the most comment bait, but the pot doesn't answer 'could you tell?' and we can't play a test, so the turn risks a bait-and-switch.
The hottest question and the best comment bait, but it promises a listening test we can't play, so line 2 must turn to the plays by ~3 s or it reads as bait.
Frame 0 is the fact file's scoped blind-test wording and the question is the fuss itself, but the mechanism isn't in it, so the payoff needs a hard turn.
The biggest scroll-stop here, but it promises an ear test the video can't run (no AI audio allowed) and the pot can't answer; it's the fuss, not the core, so use it as a beat.

line: A man got 18 months for having bots play his AI songs.
frame0: PRISON FOR HAVING BOTS PLAY HIS SONGS
emotion: Surprise, then a moral itch: 'prison, for that? Who did he even hurt?' Robots playing a man's own songs sounds victimless, so a normal viewer has to find out who got robbed, and a real, recent sentence makes it instantly believable.
backing: FL 1.8 (its own safe wording), 4.9 (18 months, sentenced 2026-10-06), 4.10 (prosecutors: hundreds of thousands of AI songs, billions of bot plays, paid for years), 3.1-3.3 and 3.7 (the shared pot); pair any harm claim with 4.14-4.15 and 8.6 (contested: never 'stole $8M from artists'); 7.10 (no AI tool named).
fixes: Keep the line; cover: BOTS PLAYED HIS AI SONGS. 18 MONTHS.
Same line; frame 0: PRISON FOR HAVING BOTS PLAY HIS AI SONGS
Keep the line; frame 0: 18 MONTHS FOR HAVING BOTS PLAY HIS AI SONGS.
notes: One real person, a real sentence and the itch 'who did he even hurt?' that leads straight to the pot; the truest strong hook here, held back only by a clunky cover that drops 'AI'.
Fresh, true, one real case with a built-in 'who did he even hurt?' that walks straight into the pot, but frame 0 leaves out AI, the fuss word.
The fact file's own safe wording about one real person; frame 0 should keep 'AI' and '18 months', and the payoff has to air that his harm is contested.

One real person, a fresh peg and the fact lock's own wording, and 'prison for that? who did he hurt?' leads to the pot, but the honest answer is contested (his lawyers, Spotify's ~$60,000), so the 'oh' lands softer, and frame 0 should keep 'AI'.

line: Who pays when bots play AI songs?
frame0: WHO PAYS WHEN BOTS PLAY AI SONGS?
emotion: Suspicion with an itch. People assume a fake play is a harmless prank or the app's problem, so the question makes them guess. The answer is the real musicians who share the same pot, and that flips it into 'wait, that's not fair'. It rides the AI-song fuss and asks the viewer directly.
backing: FL 2.4-2.5 (on one app, up to 85% of fully AI tracks' plays were fake in 2025, and fake plays are the main reason AI songs get uploaded; Deezer's numbers only); 3.1-3.3 (no per-play rate; a shared pot per country per month); 4.1-4.2 + 3.13 (caught fakes earn nothing; Apple puts that money back in the pool); 3.9-3.10 (most AI tracks never reach Spotify's pay line); 6.4 ('This is a zero-sum game'); 8.2 + 8.1 (some slip through; nobody knows how many or how much).
notes: Short, true, and the whole video is its answer, but a riddle needs the frame-0 picture to bring the jolt.
The cleanest question to the viewer: true, a sticky pays/plays rhyme, AI up front, and the answer is the mechanism, though the jolt is curiosity, not anger.
The safest strong line: no claim to attack, it rides the AI fuss, and the honest answer (nobody if caught, every real artist a sliver if not) is the payoff.
The story's core question, short, rhyming and true, with the honest two-part answer as the 'oh', but it isn't a claim, so frame 0 doesn't state the payoff and the picture has to bring the jolt.

line: Bots are skimming your favorite artist's pay.
frame0: BOTS ARE SKIMMING YOUR FAVORITE ARTIST'S PAY
emotion: Protective anger on behalf of someone you love. 'Skimming' is the hand-in-the-till feeling everyone gets instantly, and it is honest about size: small, sneaky and ongoing. Nobody likes a cheat being paid out of an honest worker's pocket.
backing: FL 3.2-3.3 (pay = your share of all plays in a monthly shared pot); 3.6 ('artists get paid from the pot' is fair shorthand); 3.7 + 7.4 (Spotify: more streams, smaller share; spam 'can dilute the royalty pool'); 7.6 (Deezer, Oct 2026: fraud 'undermines payments to legitimate artists'); 4.1-4.2 (caught fakes earn nothing, so only the ones that slip through skim); 8.2 + 8.5 + 4.10 + 7.3 (some slip through: Smith ran about 7 years on four services, and detection 'will only get harder'); 8.1 ('skimming' claims no size). Guard: bots play their own songs, never the viewer's playlist.
fixes: Bots playing AI songs are skimming your favorite artist's pay.
Bots can skim your favorite artist's pay.
Bots can skim your favorite artist's pay.
notes: The plainest bold claim, with the payoff on frame 0 and 'skimming' sizing it honestly; it asserts that fakes slip through now (FL 8.2 allows that), and AI has to arrive in line 2.
Plain, direct, states the payoff and 'skimming' is honest about size, but with no AI it drops the fuss the topic was picked for.
Punchy, and 'skim' is honest about size, but 'are skimming' asserts uncaught fraud nobody has measured, exactly where a fact-checker attacks.
The strongest gut of the pot lines, and 'skimming' is honest about size, but 'are' asserts an ongoing loss nobody has measured where L5's 'can' stays safe.

line: Bots can shrink your favorite artist's paycheck.
frame0: BOTS CAN SHRINK YOUR FAVORITE ARTIST'S PAYCHECK
emotion: Protective indignation plus a 'how?': nearly everyone has a favorite artist they want paid fairly, and robots reaching that pay without touching their songs sounds impossible, so the viewer stays for the trick; the 'you' is natural because the loss is the artist's, never the viewer's.
backing: FL 3.2-3.3, 3.7 (Spotify: 'as total streams grow, you need more streams to maintain the same share'), 7.4 (Spotify: spam 'can dilute the royalty pool'), 6.4 (Apple: 'This is a zero-sum game'), 4.1-4.2, 8.2 ('can': only uncaught fakes), 8.1 and 7.6 (size unmeasured, Deezer calls it 'minimal on Deezer': the payoff says 'a little'), 3.6 ('paycheck' is fair shorthand).
fixes: Bots playing AI songs can shrink your favorite artist's pay.
Bots playing AI songs can shrink your favorite artist's pay.
Bots playing AI songs can shrink your favorite artist's paycheck.
Bots playing AI songs can shrink your favorite artist's pay.
notes: Plain, personal and true with the payoff on frame 0, but 'can' and 'paycheck' soften the cover and AI is missing.
Plain, true and states the payoff, but 'can' softens the jolt and there's no AI to hook the fuss.
Plain, true with 'can', payoff on frame 0; the video must size 'shrink' as a little, by an amount nobody has measured.

Plain, direct and personal in the shape of the owner's v3 pick, true thanks to 'can', and 'how do bots shrink a paycheck without touching the songs?' is exactly what the pot answers; it only lacks the AI fuss.

line: You might already like an AI song.
frame0: YOU MIGHT ALREADY LIKE AN AI SONG
emotion: A small 'wait, which one?' jolt. It accuses nobody and claims nothing about your playlist. It just says out loud what people half-suspect after a blind test that 97% failed and AI tracks with millions of plays, and it sends you back through the songs you've saved.
backing: FL 5.1 and 8.7 (in a blind test, 97% of 9,000 people couldn't tell); FL 5.6 (an AI cover drew 14M+ Spotify plays in its first month; words only, never played); FL 5.7 (an AI 'band' with 550,000+ monthly listeners); FL 5.5 (Sweden's No. 1 Spotify song was mainly AI). 'Might' keeps it a possibility, never a claim about anyone's playlist. The fairness turn rests on FL 5.13 and 7.4 ('all music is treated equally'), the money turn on FL 3.2-3.3, 3.11, 4.1-4.2 and 8.2.
fixes: You might already like an AI song, and that's not the problem.
notes: The cleanest, most natural 'you' line here, but it promises a reveal about your taste and the video is about fake plays.
A great personal jolt that promises a 'which song?' reveal the pot story can't give, so the turn reads as bait.
True and the fairest to AI-using artists, but the video can't answer 'which one?' and the hook points away from the mechanism.
A fun jolt, but the payoff has to say 'that part is fine', which defuses its own line, and the video can't play a single one of the songs.

line: An AI song nobody hears can still make money.
frame0: AI SONGS NOBODY HEARS CAN MAKE MONEY
emotion: Unfairness wrapped in curiosity: it breaks the rule everyone takes for granted (no listeners, no money), and the instant follow-up is 'whose money?', which is exactly where real artists come in.
backing: FL 3.1-3.3 (no per-play rate; one shared pot per country per month, split by share of plays), FL 3.7 (more plays in the pot, smaller slices for everyone else), FL 2.4 (most plays on fully AI tracks were fake in 2025, on one app), FL 4.10 (Smith took in $14M+ from bot plays on AI songs over 7 years before he was charged). 'Can', never 'does': caught fakes earn nothing (FL 4.1-4.2, 4.4), most AI tracks never reach Spotify's 1,000-plays-a-year pay line (FL 3.9-3.10), and how much slips through is unknown (FL 8.2).
fixes: An AI song nobody hears can still get paid.
An AI song no human hears can still get paid.
An AI song no real person hears can still get paid.
notes: A clean, true paradox that rides AI and points at 'whose money?', with a softer sting than the top lines.
A good paradox that leads to 'how?', though 'nobody hears' blurs into 'nobody plays', and a song nobody plays earns nothing.
True with 'can', but the hear/play hinge needs 'fake plays' in line 2, or leavers think unheard songs earn just by existing.
A true paradox ('hears', not 'plays', is the right distinction) whose 'whose money?' leads to the pot, but frame 0 names no victim and can read as a side-hustle hook.
